items.title: Dominic James "Nick" La Rocca Interview, 1959-06-14
items.q: I've done a little research as well. I've done some technical work on his so-called recordings... there is no sign of any records of Buddy Bolden... his prowess, if any, must remain a beautiful legend, a fairy story

ctx.x: Today is Sunday, June 14th, 1959. This is Brian Rust of London, England. I'm sitting in the living room of Nick LaRocca's home, 2218 Constance Street, New Orleans, Louisiana. Mr LaRocca has done me the honour of making a tape recording of his voice telling his story of how he came to create jazz and his opinions and the whole story of the growth of the music. And he's asked me to give my side of it, how I came to be interested in the music and what it means to me and to English people now. Until 1936, I'd never…

it's easy enough to listen to them. I've only got to listen to those and compare them with the original Dixieland Jazz Band to realise that the one is Ragtime and the other is Jazz. The original Dixieland Jazz Band isn't called Jazz for Nothing. There are other musicians having laid claim to having made the first jazz records. I have just compiled a book which lays great stress on the dates of recordings. The first jazz recordings in the book, not Ragtime, the first jazz recordings, are those by the original…

items.title: Dominic James "Nick" La Rocca Interview, 1958-06-16
items.q: I never knew nothing about this Negro Bolin until he's history and started digging from Negro mythology and tales that I don't know where they get him.

ctx.x: Pioneer of jazz wins recognition, New Orleans, editor from New Orleans States. It was gratifying to read in your paper on February 27th the article on Nick LaRocca, famous leader of the original Dixieland jazz band. He deserves the honor accorded him and his band by the Jazz Club of England whose leader, Marcus O'Donoghau visited our sea last summer. If Mr. LaRocca accepts this invitation, and I hope he does, I'm sure he will mention some of the other bands that played jazz at that time. Tom Brown, who took his…

I'd like to comment on the dates that she has here to show you she was eaten up, taken in by this communist propaganda. I wish you'd hear this tape recorder. Buddy Bolin, Freddie Kepler, George Pequet left here in 1911. In 1906, by the things that I have in my hand, from Louisiana State Mental Hospital at Jackson, Louisiana, Bolin was incarcerated in there in 1906. He couldn't have played with them. And I've told you when these Negroes came it was 1917. Clarence Williams, he says, left here around 1911 or 13.…

items.title: Dominic James "Nick" La Rocca Interview, 1958-06-09
items.q: Buddy Bolden was the hottest cornetist in the world... this is before my time.

ctx.x: It is an original Negro tune, which was made up down south. It was named Tiger Rag when the Dixieland Band brought it up north. Buddy, you want me to continue with this? Yeah, go on. Buddy Bolden was the hottest cornetist in the world, and he played so much that he is in the insane asylum now if he is still living. After this time came King Oliver, Punk, and Freddie Capron, that's spelled K-E-P-P-E-R-T, and the original Creole Band. They were the last word and swing cornet players. We used to have swing sessions every morning around 3 o'clock after the boys got through with their work and each man would do his bit. Quote, the first hot band to leave from the South and introduce swing music was the Creole Jazz Band, unquote, says Mr. Williams. Quote, following the Dixieland Jazz Band, which recorded Livery Stable Blues and Tiger Ray, which swept the country. items.title: Dominic James "Nick" La Rocca Interview, 1958-06-09
items.q: The interviewee is reading a 1936 article about Buddy Bolden Cornetis from 1918, stating 'Clarence stated that he heard him play...'

ctx.x: And this is what I'd like you to read. It was in 1918. If I got 1819 down there, it's the wrong date. I wasn't even in. It would have to be 1918 that we had these Mama's Baby Boy and Brown Skin, who you fought? I want you to read this here, part of an article. He says, Swing, as they call it today, by Clarence Waino. From Honky Tonk to Swing.

All right. Let's see. This is from Orchestra World, 1936. Let's see. All right. Swing, as they call it today, was originated in New Orleans, the birthplace of Sister Kate and many other standard swing tunes, such as Tiger Rag. In those days, you could find in the slums of New Orleans such places as the Red Onion, the Keystone, Pete Lawless, and the Odd Fellows Hall, where the Eagle Band used to play.
